answerHtml:

Two identical plastic blocks are placed next to each other with Block A at a temperature of 40.0∘C40.0\ {^\circ}C and Block B at a temperature of 50.0∘C50.0\ {^\circ}C. Provide a detailed explanation of how heat exchange through radiation will eventually result in a state of thermal equilibrium between the two blocks, assuming no heat exchange with the surrounding environment.

Objects at a higher temperature will emit electromagnetic radiation at a greater rate than those at a lower temperature. 1 mark
Block B therefore emits electromagnetic radiation at a greater rate than it receives electromagnetic radiation from Block A, thereby decreasing in energy 1 mark
As the energy of Block B decreases, so does its temperature, and hence the rate at which it emits electromagnetic radiation also decreases. 1 mark

Likewise,
Block A emits electromagnetic radiation at a lower rate than it receives electromagnetic radiation from Block B, thereby increasing in energy and temperature.

As the energy of Block A increases, so does its temperature, and hence the rate at which it emits electromagnetic radiation also increases.

 1 mark
When they reach the same temperature, the two blocks will emit and receive electromagnetic radiation at equal rates, thereby remaining in thermal equilibrium. 1 mark

(a) With reference to impulse, explain why the use of a seat belt reduces the likelihood of injury. (3 marks) (b) An exception to this law is that the driver does not need to wear their seat belt while reversing. Explain, with reference to a relevant Physics principle(s), why a seat belt is not necessary as a safety feature in this case. (2 marks)
html:

(2 marks)
answerHtml:
Download original Word marking guide, including diagram layouts ↗

Seat belts are legally required to be worn by drivers in order to reduce the likelihood of injury in the event of a crash.

(a) With reference to impulse, explain why the use of a seat belt reduces the likelihood of injury.

(3 marks)

Since I=ΔpI = \Delta p, the impulse to the driver will be the same regardless of whether or not they wear a seat belt 1 mark
The stretching of the seat belt increases the time over which the driver comes to rest during the crash. 1 mark
Since I=FtI = Ft, a longer time over which the same impulse is achieved will mean a smaller average force being applied to the driver at any time (and hence less likelihood of injury). 1 mark

(b) An exception to this law is that the driver does not need to wear their seat belt while reversing. Explain, with reference to a relevant Physics principle(s), why a seat belt is not necessary as a safety feature in this case.

(2 marks)

By Newton’s first law, if a driver crashes while reversing, their body would continue to travel towards the back of the car. 1 mark
This is in the direction of their seat, rather than their seat belt. 1 mark

To do so they set up a series of speed cameras at 4.00 m intervals from a start line. They then drive a car to the start line and bring it to a stop. The diagram below shows this set-up, with the car not yet in position.

The car then accelerates from rest and its speed as it passes each camera is expected to follow the equation:

Equation 1: v2=2asv^{2} = 2as

where: vv is the speed of the car measured by the speed camera (in m s-1).

aa is the acceleration of the car (in m s-2).

ss is the distance of the speed camera from the start line (in m).

The car manufacturer has collected the following data:

ss (m) vv (m s-1) v2v^{2} ( )
4.00 8.10 65.6
8.00 11.5 131
12.0 14.1
16.0 16.2 262

(1 mark)

(b) Complete the missing value in the v2v^{2} column, expressing this to three significant figures.

(2 marks)

(c) Using the grid and axes provided on the next page, plot a graph of v2v^{2} against ss, with v2v^{2} on the vertical axis. Include a line of best fit.

(5 marks)

text: Handheld infrared thermometers Handheld infrared thermometers (HITs) have become widespread by groups mass screening people for COVID-19, such as in airports and shopping centres. HITs have largely been adopted as they are quick and easy to use, and provide a non-contact method for determining people’s temperature. Readings are generally taken from an individual’s forehead, with temperatures of 36 ∘ C 36\ {^\circ}C or higher suggestive that the person is carrying COVID-19. However, the method has largely been criticised as accurate readings require careful consideration of the distance between the HIT and the individual, as well as the angle the HIT is aimed at. Moreover, forehead temperature could be raised due to factors such as menstruation, pregnancy, or even recently having a hot drink. These temperatures could likewise be lowered from sweating or air-conditioning, or by individuals taking antipyretic drugs (lowering their body temperature). HITs determine the temperature of an object based on the thermal radiation it emits. On a particle level, the atoms that make up object contain charged particles and the random motion of these charged particles causes electromagnetic radiation to be released. When an object is at a higher temperature, it will emit radiation at a greater rate. The intensity of this radiation is known to be I = ε σ T 4 I = \varepsilon\ \sigma\ T^{4} where I I is the intensity of the emitted thermal radiation (in W m -2 ), T T is the temperature of the object (in K), and σ \sigma is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, which has a numerical value of σ = 5.67 × 10 − 8 \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{- 8} . ε \varepsilon is the emissivity of the object, a unitless measure of the object’s ability to emit and absorb thermal radiation. Some typical emissivity values are given on the next page. Aluminium Foil ε \varepsilon = 0.03 Paint ε \varepsilon = 0.90 Glass ε \varepsilon = 0.95 Skin ε \varepsilon = 0.98 Ice ε \varepsilon = 0.99 Typical emissivity values The HIT is able to measure the average intensity of thermal radiation given off by a surface’s detection area. This area depends on how far away the HIT is located with typical HITs having a spot ratio of 8:1, which suggests that from a distance of 8 m away the detection area would be a circular region that is 1 m in diameter, with the diameter changing in direct proportion to the distance. Most HITs include a laser that allows the user to see the detection area; this laser light is not involved in determining the temperature though. Based on the average intensity of thermal radiation emitted from the detection area, the temperature is calculated by assuming the object to have an emissivity of ε = 0.95 \varepsilon = 0.95 . (a) Explain why an object would emit more thermal radiation when its temperature is higher. (3 marks) (b) Based on the equation in the article, determine the units of σ \sigma . (2 marks) Units: _____________________ (c) Estimate the minimum intensity of thermal radiation given off by a person with COVID-19, showing clear working. (5 marks) _____________________ W m -2 (d) If the temperature of a typical person was recorded using a HIT, how would it be expected to compare to the true value? Circle an answer and then justify your choice. (3 marks) Less than the true value Equal to the true value Greater than the true value Justification: (e) If a HIT is used to determine a person’s temperature from a distance of 1.50 m, determine the size of the detection area. (3 marks) _____________________ m 2 (f) Discuss why the distance used in part (e) would not be appropriate for determining a forehead temperature measurement. (3 marks)

text: Radium watch dials In 1914 the Radium Luminous Material Corporation was founded, which produced a form of radio-luminescent paint containing radium-226. The paint was used in watch dials to allow the hands and indices to glow and still be read in the dark. This paint was applied by a group of young women who came to be known as the Radium Girls. The women would manually paint the watch dials using brushes. In order to achieve fine lines, these women were encouraged to lick the ends of the paint brushes in order to shape and ‘point’ them. Despite being told at the time that this practice was harmless, exposure to the radium-226 in the paint, an alpha-emitter, led to radiation poisoning. When ingested, the body stores radium in bones, similar to calcium. This can lead to bone degradation, and the ionisation of DNA molecules in cells can cause them to become cancerous. The first death of a Radium Girl was recorded in 1923, with the woman’s jaw falling away from her skull prior to her death. Radium watch dials remained in common production throughout the 20 th century, with safer radioisotopes brought into use in the 1970s and non-radioactive luminescent materials not used until the 1990s. Many radium watches are still in circulation and although the glass casing offers some protection, since radium-226 decays into a short-lived gamma emitter (with average gamma ray energies of approximately 950 keV), the watches still pose a safety risk to people. Moreover, since radium-226 has a half-life of 1600 years, the activity of these watches will have barely decreased since they were first manufactured, being approximately 37 kBq. This means that a person wearing a radium watch will receive a significant dose equivalent from gamma ray exposure. (a) Write the nuclear equation for the radioactive decay of radium-226. (2 marks) (b) Discuss why the Radium Girls’ practice of licking paint brushes led to a high incidence of cancer. (3 marks) (c) Show that the activity of a watch dial painted in the Radium Luminous Material Corporation’s first year would have only decreased by approximately 5% by today. (2 marks) (d) Explain why someone wearing a radium watch is only at risk due to the gamma radiation emitted. (3 marks) (e) Estimate the dose equivalent received by someone wearing a radium watch over the course of a year. Assume that the wearer absorbs 25% of all emitted gamma rays, localised to their hand (of mass 0.50 kg). Show full working. (7 marks) _____________________ Sv
